web_title: 3. Distribution, Supply Chain & Unit Economics ($100 Operating Waterfall + ETF Drag Mechanics)
book_title: Chapter 3: The Brutal Physics of a $100 Server Dollar and a $100 ETF Dollar

epigraph.quote: In capital-intensive infrastructure, the income statement tells you what management hopes happened; the cash flow statement tells you what the power grid and chip vendor demanded upfront.
epigraph.author: Forensic Capital Allocation Rule

web_blocks.html: Unit economics in the NBIL/NBIS ecosystem operate at two distinct levels: the physical supply chain of Nebius Group N.V., and the frictional fee-and-volatility drag of the GraniteShares 2x ETF wrapper. On the physical side, Nebius sits between two powerful choke points: NVIDIA on the silicon supply side, and regional utilities and data-center landlords on the power-and-real-estate side [16][30]. Drawing on its Yandex hyperscale heritage, Nebius bypasses OEM markups (such as Dell or HPE) by co-designing custom server boards, liquid-cooling manifolds, and rack architectures directly with Asian ODMs [16]. This hardware engineering trims unit capex per megawatt relative to generic buyers, yet GPUs still require upfront cash while cloud revenue arrives over 36 to 60 months [30].

On the go-to-market side, Nebius runs a bifurcated model. The first tier is a self-serve developer cloud targeting AI startups and mid-market firms (such as Shopify and Cloudflare) with hourly GPU pricing and API provisioning [21][27]. The second—and now dominant—tier consists of bespoke multi-year hyperscaler contracts with Microsoft and Meta [13][14]. Nebius has used these investment-grade deals to reshape working capital, as upfront customer prepayments lifted FY2025 CFO to $401.9 million despite a $(611.7) million GAAP operating loss [29][31]. However, as the audited FY2025 waterfall demonstrates, positive CFO is dwarfed by the capital expenditure required to build the clusters.

web_blocks.caption: NBIS Audited FY2025 Unit Economics: What Happens to Every $100 of Revenue
web_blocks.takeaway: On every $100 of FY2025 revenue ($529.8M total), Nebius incurred $31.37 in COGS, $33.47 in R&D/product engineering, $74.37 in SG&A/other opex, and $76.26 in D&A—producing an operating loss of -$115.46 per $100. Customer prepayments lifted CFO to +$75.86 per $100, but $767.46 of CapEx ($4,066.0M) resulted in -$691.60 of Free Cash Flow per $100 of revenue.

web_blocks.html: NBIS's physical unit economics reflect a 7.67x CapEx-to-Revenue ratio in FY2025 and a projected ~8x–9x ratio in FY2026 (~$27 billion CapEx on ~$3.0–$3.4 billion revenue) [17][31]. An investor in NBIL faces a second layer of steep friction inside the ETF wrapper. Audited June 30, 2026 GraniteShares N-CSR statements and NBIL's October 28, 2026 Form 497K reveal four compounding drags on every $100 invested [42][43]. First is the explicit 1.41% net operating expense ratio (1.30% management fee, 0.12% other expenses, and 0.03% LBOX acquired fees, less 0.04% waiver; capped at 1.50% through Dec 31, 2027) [43]. Second is an explicit 1.45% estimated indirect swap cost disclosed in the October 28, 2026 497K footnote, taking combined prospectus expense estimates to 2.86% [43]. Third is an audited OBFR01 + 600 bps (6.00% spread) floating rate on the Clear Street, LLC total return swap ($187.54 million notional at June 30, 2026) [42]. That spread exceeds the 100–250 bps prime-rate baseline by more than triple, imposing roughly -$6.00 to -$7.50 per $100 of net swap drag after T-bill offset [42]. Fourth is daily volatility decay, approximated by 0.5 × L × (L - 1) × σ² (or exp(-σ²) - 1) where L = 2 and σ is NBIS's annualized volatility [5]. NBIL's June 30, 2026 N-CSR also shows $191.81 million in distributable earnings ($203.81M unrealized swap appreciation vs. $3.79M paid-in capital and $97 carryforwards), exposing taxable holders to lumpy year-end RIC distributions [42].

web_blocks.caption: NBIL Wrapper Economics: Audited Fee, OBFR+600 bps Swap Drag & Volatility Decay on $100 (Assuming Flat 0% NBIS Return)
headers: Audited Swap Financing Drag (OBFR+600 bps Net Est.)
web_blocks.takeaway: Audited N-CSR swap terms (OBFR01 + 600 bps with Clear Street) plus the 497K's 1.45% indirect swap cost raise NBIL's non-volatility wrapper drag to roughly -$8.86 to -$10.36 per $100 annually—pushing total 1-year erosion on a flat 0% NBIS year to ~$56–$74 at 80%–100% volatility.

web_blocks.html: The revised table above rests directly on NBIL's audited N-CSR swap schedule and October 2026 prospectus [1][42][43]. Annual explicit fees, indirect swap costs, and OBFR+600 bps financing add up to ~9%–10% of yearly friction. Combining that toll with quadratic variance drag exp(-σ²) - 1 at 80%–100%+ volatility creates a massive hurdle [5][42]. Even when NBIS executes well, sideways chop or sharp pullbacks leave the 2x daily ETF permanently behind a 2x point-to-point move [5].

A closer look at Nebius's asset-light partnership shift in Q3 2026 also shows how unit economics evolve under capital pressure [17][47]. Funding 100% of a $27 billion (2026) and $40B–$45B (2027) CapEx roadmap on its own balance sheet would strain capital markets. Nebius therefore structured asset-light partnerships—generating $325.1 million of point-in-time Q3 2026 revenue—where third-party capital or hyperscalers fund 75% to 85% of upfront hardware and facility costs [17][35][47]. While this model lowers Nebius's direct cash outlay per megawatt, it shares long-term upside with financing partners and creates lumpier milestone revenue.

Finally, unit economics in GPU-as-a-Service depend heavily on cluster utilization and payback compression [34]. Management highlights average contract values above $25 million per megawatt, noting that upfront customer prepayments shorten cash payback on dedicated hyperscaler builds [13][34]. However, self-serve clusters carry no long-term take-or-pay floor. If spot GPU rental rates soften as global supply catches demand, uncontracted capacity faces margin compression while fixed colocation leases, power commitments, and convertible-debt interest remain rigid. Inside NBIL, daily swap rebalancing locks in losses during sharp underlying drawdowns before spot rates recover [5].

web_blocks.title: Supply Chain Bottlenecks: From Silicon to Megawatts
paragraphs: Even with NVIDIA backing and custom ODM server designs, Nebius's unit economics remain hostage to physical grid infrastructure. In Vineland, New Jersey—the anchor site for the Microsoft contract—grid interconnect constraints forced a shift toward on-site Bloom Energy fuel cells, pushing some capacity commissioning into late 2026 and early 2027 and prompting management to guide FY2026 revenue to the low end of its $3.0B–$3.4B range [16][17].

book_paragraphs: To see why NBIL is such a treacherous long-term vehicle, you and I have to trace a single hundred-dollar bill through two different machines: first through Nebius Group's operating business, and second through GraniteShares' daily-reset ETF wrapper.

Start with Nebius Group's audited 2025 financials, where total revenue came in at 529.8 million dollars. Imagine shrinking that entire year down to one hundred dollars of revenue. Out of that hundred dollars, Nebius spent 31 dollars and 37 cents on direct cost of revenues—electricity, colocation, and data center operations. It spent another 33 dollars and 47 cents on product development and engineering payroll, and 74 dollars and 37 cents on sales, general, administrative, and other operating expenses. Then came the elephant in the room: 76 dollars and 26 cents of depreciation and amortization on its rapidly expanding fleet of NVIDIA GPUs. Add it all up, and for every hundred dollars of revenue Nebius booked in 2025, it posted an operating loss of 115 dollars and 46 cents.

Now here is where things get interesting. On the cash flow statement, Nebius actually generated 75 dollars and 86 cents of positive operating cash flow for every hundred dollars of revenue. How does a company with a massive operating loss generate positive operating cash flow? Through customer prepayments and deferred revenue. Hyperscalers and large enterprise clients paid cash upfront to lock in future GPU capacity. Yet even with those upfront prepayments, Nebius spent 767 dollars and 46 cents on capital expenditures for every hundred dollars of revenue—buying GPUs, transformers, liquid-cooling racks, and data center shells. That left free cash flow at negative 691 dollars and 60 cents per hundred dollars of revenue.

book_subsections.title: The Second Machine: How $100 Erodes Inside NBIL
paragraphs: Now take a separate hundred-dollar bill and place it inside NBIL, and look at what the audited SEC filings actually reveal—because the real friction is far worse than Wall Street rules of thumb suggest. First, NBIL deducts an explicit net operating expense ratio of 1.41 percent per year (capped at 1.50 percent excluding interest and derivative costs). Second, NBIL's October 28, 2026 summary prospectus discloses an additional 1.45 percent in estimated indirect swap expenses that do not even appear in the headline fee table—putting combined direct and indirect fee drag at 2.86 percent before financing spreads. Third, and most shocking, GraniteShares' audited June 30, 2026 N-CSR reveals that NBIL's sole total return swap with Clear Street, LLC carries a floating rate of OBFR01 plus 600 basis points—six full percentage points of spread over the overnight bank funding rate, nearly triple the 100 to 250 basis point spread typical of liquid mega-cap swaps. That translates into roughly six to seven and a half dollars of annual net financing drag on every hundred dollars before the underlying stock even moves.

Those financing charges, however, still pale beside volatility decay. For a two-times daily ETF, the mathematical drag from daily rebalancing grows with the square of the underlying stock's volatility. If Nebius Group finishes a twelve-month stretch completely flat—zero percent total return—but experiences 80 percent annualized volatility along the way, daily compounding math plus NBIL's audited fees and OBFR-plus-600-basis-point swap spread erode your hundred-dollar bill down to roughly forty-two to forty-four dollars. At 100 percent annualized volatility, it erodes down to roughly twenty-six to twenty-eight dollars. You can be dead right about the long-term direction of AI infrastructure and still lose more than half your principal to the calendar and the swap desk.

And notice one more physical bottleneck in Nebius's unit economics: power. In Vineland, New Jersey, where Nebius is building out its flagship Microsoft cluster, electrical grid interconnect delays forced the company to pivot partially toward on-site Bloom Energy fuel cells, pushing some capacity commissioning into late 2026 and early 2027. Every time a transformer or utility hookup slips by a quarter, revenue gets pushed into next year while depreciation, interest expense, and corporate overhead keep ticking—and inside NBIL, those quarterly timing shocks get magnified by two every single afternoon.

book_subsections.title: The Asset-Light Pivot and Spot-Pricing Vulnerability
paragraphs: To manage a twenty-seven-billion-dollar CapEx bill in 2026 and a forty-to-forty-five-billion-dollar bill in 2027, Nebius has begun leaning on asset-light partnerships and upfront customer prepayments to cover seventy-five to eighty-five percent of new buildouts. That is smart financial engineering—it shifts part of the hardware financing burden onto hyperscalers and third-party capital providers. Yet there is no free lunch in infrastructure: sharing the upfront bill means sharing the long-term economics, and milestone-based partnership revenue makes quarterly results much lumpier.

At the same time, you and I have to watch the difference between contracted clusters and spot capacity. Dedicated hyperscaler contracts carry multi-year commitments, but any uncontracted GPU clusters sold on an hourly self-serve basis are exposed to spot pricing. If industry-wide GPU supply catches up to demand, hourly rental rates fall fast—while power leases, server depreciation, and interest obligations stay locked in place.

Put both halves of Chapter 3 side by side so the unit economics are unmistakable. On the operating side, Nebius spent 767 dollars and 46 cents of CapEx for every 100 dollars of revenue it earned in 2025, leaving free cash flow at negative 691 dollars and 60 cents per 100 dollars of sales. On the ETF wrapper side, NBIL layers a 1.41 to 1.50 percent fee cap, swap financing spreads, and quadratic volatility decay on top of that cash-burning buildout. That double friction is why you must never mistake top-line GPU demand for self-funding economic compounding.

Think of it like owning a fleet of delivery trucks where every truck costs ten times your annual freight revenue, and you have to buy a new fleet every three years just to stay competitive. Even if your customers prepay their shipping contracts upfront, your bank account only stays full as long as lenders and equity investors keep writing checks. And if you wrap that trucking business inside a daily-reset two-times derivative contract, every bump in the highway shakes loose a little more of your principal that never comes back.

book_callouts.title: Mentor Check: Prepayments Are Not Free Cash Flow
book_callouts.quote: Customer prepayments finance the shovel, not the profit; you still have to deliver the compute for five years while the hardware depreciates.
book_callouts.text: When you and I look at Nebius's $100 waterfall, remember that positive operating cash flow built on customer prepayments is borrowed from future service delivery, while the -$691.60 of Free Cash Flow per $100 of revenue has to be plugged by debt and equity markets.
